To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the lifetime risk of developing breast cancer in a woman who has had a first breast cancer diagnosed before age 50 is 29%, and that a 50-year-old breast cancer survivor has a 1.6% chance of developing a new breast cancer each year.
the lifetime risk of a breast cancer survivor developing a second primary breast cancer was 7.4% at age 65 and that the lifetime risk for the general population was 12.3% at age 70.
1. The lifetime risk of breast cancer in a woman with a first primary breast cancer is 30% to 50% higher than that in a woman without breast cancer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and evaluation of new methods to improve the quality and cost-effectiveness of health care.
the development of a new method for the estimation of breast cancer survival rates in the presence of competing causes of death.
the development and implementation of a new technology for the detection and treatment of breast cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

breast cancer screening in women with a history of breast cancer has not been studied in randomized controlled trials, and therefore the evidence does not support or refute the effectiveness of breast cancer screening in this population.
the evidence for a survival benefit from screening mammography for women with a personal history of breast cancer is limited and inconclusive.
there are no studies to suggest that screening mammograms are not effective in detecting breast cancer in the second breast in women with a history of breast cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are not doing a good job of screening breast cancer survivors.
there is a need for more research on surveillance mammography in this population.
the lifetime risk of breast cancer is higher for survivors of early stage breast cancer than for women in the general population.

we need to do a better job of educating women and their providers about the risks and benefits of annual mammography.
